lessons.title: The Working Capital Cycle: Inventory, Receivable and Payable Days Calculated Step by Step

children.text: Chapter 1 gave you working capital in rupees. Rupees are hard to compare: a ₹58 crore receivable book is enormous for one company and trivial for another. Days fix that. Convert every line into the number of days it represents and you can compare a Morbi tile maker with Hindustan Unilever on the same scale.

This is the single most useful calculation in the course, and it takes four formulas. We will work through every one of them on the same balance sheet you already know, then apply them to three real listed companies.

body.caption: Days Inventory Outstanding: how long stock sits before it is sold
Days Sales Outstanding: how long customers take to pay
Days Payable Outstanding: how long the business takes to pay suppliers
Cash Conversion Cycle: the days the business funds itself

children.text: use cost figures, because inventory and payables are recorded at cost.

uses sales, because receivables are recorded at selling price including the margin. Mixing these up is the most common error in working capital analysis, and the next section shows exactly how much damage it does.

markDefs.definition: Days Inventory Outstanding. How many days of production cost sits in raw material, work in progress and finished goods before it is sold.
Days Payable Outstanding. The average number of days the business takes to pay its own suppliers.
Days Sales Outstanding. The average number of days between raising an invoice and collecting the cash.

children.text: Step by Step on One Balance Sheet

Sunrise Ceramics Ltd, FY2026: inventories ₹42 crore, trade receivables ₹58 crore, trade payables ₹42 crore. From its profit and loss statement: sales ₹180 crore, cost of goods sold ₹126 crore, and raw material purchases for the year ₹96 crore.

body.title: What those numbers mean in real time

events.title: Clay and glaze arrive
events.description: The supplier's invoice is dated today. Nothing has been paid, and nothing has been sold.

events.title: The tiles are sold
events.description: Inventory has sat for about 122 days as raw material, work in progress and finished stock. An invoice is raised on the dealer.

events.title: Suppliers are paid
events.description: On average Sunrise takes about 160 days to pay, well beyond the 45 days agreed with most vendors. Cash leaves here.

events.title: The dealer pays
events.description: Another 118 days pass before collection. Cash comes back in.

events.title: 79.6 days of self-funding
events.description: From paying suppliers to collecting from dealers, Sunrise funds roughly 80 days of its own operations out of its own capital and its bank limit.

body.label: What 79.6 days costs in rupees
body.context: At sales of ₹180 crore a year, one day of sales is about ₹0.49 crore. Multiply by the 79.6-day cycle and that is the cash permanently locked in operations.

body.text: This conversion is the most practical thing in the lesson. Cutting the cycle by 10 days releases about ₹4.9 crore of cash for this company, permanently, without selling anything extra or raising a rupee of new funding.

body.title: Run the full calculation yourself
body.prompt: A Kolhapur foundry reports inventories of ₹18 crore, trade receivables of ₹27 crore and trade payables of ₹15 crore, on sales of ₹120 crore and cost of goods sold of ₹90 crore. Using cost of goods sold as the denominator for both inventory and payable days, what is its cash conversion cycle in days? Round to the nearest day.
body.explanation: Inventory days are 18 / 90 x 365 = 73. Receivable days are 27 / 120 x 365 = 82. Payable days are 15 / 90 x 365 = 61. The cycle is 73 + 82 - 61 = 94 days. The foundry funds roughly three months of its own operations.

children.text: Look at what happens if you compute payable days against cost of goods sold instead of purchases. Payables of ₹42 crore against COGS of ₹126 crore gives 121.7 days instead of 159.7 days, and the cycle changes from 79.6 days to 117.6 days. The same balance sheet, 38 days apart.

columns.label: The purist version
points: Inventory days against cost of goods sold
Payable days against credit purchases for the year
Receivable days against credit sales, not total sales
Opening and closing balances averaged rather than closing alone
Best when you have the full annual report and the notes

columns.label: The practical version
points: Inventory and payable days both against cost of goods sold
What most screening tools, including screener.in, effectively do
Fine for comparing companies, as long as you apply it identically to each

body.text: Consistency matters more than purity. If you compute one company the purist way and its competitor the practical way, your comparison is worthless. Pick one method, state it, and apply it to every company in the set.

children.text: Credit sales, not total sales. If only 85% of Sunrise's ₹180 crore of sales are on credit, the right denominator for receivable days is ₹153 crore, and DSO rises from 117.6 to 138.4 days. For a business with a large cash counter, such as a jeweller or a restaurant chain, using total sales badly understates how slowly its credit customers actually pay.

Average, not closing balances. Inventory at Sunrise opened the year at ₹36 crore and closed at ₹42 crore. Using the average of ₹39 crore gives 113 inventory days instead of 121.7. For seasonal businesses, where the 31 March stock position is nothing like the position in October, the average is far more honest. For a business with a spiky year end, always check both.

body.title: Get the denominator right
body.textWithBlank: Receivable days are calculated using sales in the denominator, while inventory days use ___ of goods sold, because inventory is recorded at cost rather than at selling price.
body.explanation: Inventory and payables sit on the balance sheet at cost, so they must be compared with a cost figure. Receivables include the profit margin, so they are compared with sales.

children.text: Here are the FY2026 figures reported in the ratios section of screener.in for three very different Indian businesses. Every number below is days.

body.caption: The same three companies, cycle computed (days, FY2026)

children.text: Hindustan Unilever gets about 169 days from its suppliers while turning stock in 61 days and collecting in 19, so its cycle is about -89 days. Its suppliers fund its operations. DMart holds 37 days of stock but collects at the till in about 1 day, so even with only 8 days of supplier credit its cycle is around 30 days. Titan carries 222 days of gold and design inventory, which no amount of counter collection can offset, giving a cycle of about 211 days.

body.text: Screener reports DMart's cash conversion cycle as 29 days while these three components add to 30. Small differences like that come from rounding each component before adding. Never chase the last day; the shape of the cycle is what matters.

stats.label: Suppliers fund the cycle
stats.context: Negative cycle: cash arrives before bills fall due

stats.label: Customers fund the cycle
stats.context: Near-instant collection offsets most of the stock

stats.label: The business funds itself
stats.context: Inventory dominates and must be financed

body.title: Read the cycle
body.question: A company reports inventory days of 40, debtor days of 65 and payable days of 120. What does its cash conversion cycle tell you?
options: The cycle is 225 days and the company is in serious trouble
The cycle is negative at -15 days, so suppliers are effectively funding its operations
The cycle is 15 days and the company funds two weeks of operations itself
The cycle cannot be computed without the current ratio
body.explanation: 40 plus 65 minus 120 is -15 days. The company collects from customers and sells its stock before its own supplier bills fall due, so suppliers fund the working capital. This is normal for large FMCG companies and organised retailers with strong bargaining power.

body.title: Same cycle, different problem
body.scenario: Two auto component makers each report a cash conversion cycle of 90 days. Company A has inventory days of 95, debtor days of 20 and payable days of 25. Company B has inventory days of 20, debtor days of 100 and payable days of 30.
body.prompt: Are these two companies facing the same working capital problem? What would you investigate at each, and which is easier to fix?
body.modelAnswer:
Same total, completely different problems.

Company A is a stock problem. Ninety-five days of inventory means over three months of production sitting in stores, work in progress and finished goods. Investigate the mix: is it slow-moving spares, a wide stock keeping unit range, poor production planning, or deliberate stocking against a supply risk? The fixes are operational, such as tighter reorder levels, ABC classification and shorter production runs, and they are largely within the company's own control.

Company B is a collection problem. A hundred days against agreed terms that are probably 45 or 60 means either weak collection discipline or customers with real bargaining power, likely large original equipment manufacturers. Investigate the ageing schedule, concentration by customer, and whether the delay is disputes, paperwork or deliberate stretching.

Which is easier to fix? Company A's, usually. Inventory decisions are internal, while collection depends on the customer's willingness to pay, and a supplier who pushes a dominant buyer too hard can lose the account. Company B also has a financing route the other lacks: if its buyers are large corporates, its invoices may be discountable on a TReDS platform, which converts those receivables to cash without a fight. Both are covered in Chapters 4 and 6.

body.title: Compute a cash conversion cycle for any company
steps: Take inventories, trade receivables and trade payables from the balance sheet, and note whether you are using closing or average balances.
Take sales and cost of goods sold from the profit and loss statement, and find purchases in the notes if you want the purist payable days.
Compute inventory days as inventory divided by cost of goods sold, times 365.
Compute receivable days as receivables divided by sales, times 365, and use credit sales instead if a large share of sales is cash.
Compute payable days on the same cost base you chose, and stay consistent across every company you compare.
Add inventory days and receivable days, then subtract payable days.
Repeat for the previous three or four years, because the trend matters more than the level.
Multiply the cycle by daily sales to convert the answer back into rupees of trapped cash.

body.text: The cash conversion cycle is the working capital number you can act on. Every day you cut from it releases one day of sales in cash, permanently, without a single extra rupee of revenue.

body.label: Ratios section on screener.in
body.description: Scroll to the Ratios table for debtor days, inventory days, days payable and the cash conversion cycle across a decade. Pull up a company you know, compute the cycle by hand from its balance sheet, and see how close you land.

points: Inventory days use cost of goods sold, receivable days use sales, and payable days use purchases or cost of goods sold, because each balance sheet line is recorded on a different basis.
The cash conversion cycle is inventory days plus receivable days minus payable days, and it measures how many days the business funds itself.
Changing the payable days denominator shifted this company's cycle by 38 days, so state your method and apply it consistently.
Multiply the cycle by daily sales to convert days into the rupees of cash locked in the business.
Averaging opening and closing balances, and using credit sales rather than total sales, gives a more honest answer for seasonal or counter-sale businesses.
Two companies with the same cycle can have opposite problems, so always read the three components separately before drawing a conclusion.
